title: Effectiveness of Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop Generate–Validate–Repair for Natural‑Language → Configuration Translation in Emulated Multi‑Device Networks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory evaluation (N=200 paired multi‑device intents) to measure whether a bounded generate–validate–repair pipeline that places a formal verifier (Batfish) in the loop reduces semantic configuration errors versus a single‑pass LLM generation. Execution used containerized FRRouting/VyOS images, Batfish verification, a deterministic task generator, and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The preregistered execution used a shared initial LLM candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). In the confirmatory cohort the shared initial candidate was identical to both baseline and guarded responses for all confirmatory pairs (200/200), and no verifier‑guided repairs were applied (repair attempts = 0/200). Consequently the paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv), the exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0, and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000) is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00]. Because the preregistered shared_initial_generation design produced identical initial candidates across conditions, the preregistered primary paired test is uninformative for detecting marginal verifier repair effects in this confirmatory cohort. We (1) state the deterministic validator decision rule used to assign verifier_pass, (2) report the archival counts and artifact references that substantiate the ceiling effect and zero repair attempts, (3) explain why McNemar/bootstrap inference is vacuous under zero discordant pairs and relate this to the preregistered detectability tradeoff, and (4) present representative difficulty diagnostics from archived exemplars to contextualize the constrained result.

sections.introduction: Generative language models have been proposed to translate operator intent into device configuration changes for NetOps. Prior work advocates closed‑loop, verifier‑assisted pipelines to reduce semantic outages caused by unsafe ordering, reachability violations, or hallucinated commands. We preregistered a paired experiment (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) to measure the marginal value of a verifier‑guided repair stage: does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using a formal verifier (Batfish) reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations relative to a single LLM generation? Our contribution is a fully archived, preregistered paired test that reports artifact‑grounded outcomes, describes the deterministic validator decision rule, and explains how a principled design choice (shared_initial_generation) produced a ceiling effect that rendered the preregistered primary test uninformative for marginal repair detection.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and benchmarks document active research on LLMs and agentic pipelines for NetOps and AIOps and propose verifier‑assisted workflows for reachability and policy checking. Formal verification tools (e.g., Batfish, header‑space engines, SMT‑based verifiers) are standard validators for many semantic properties; executable benchmark efforts show LLM outputs can fail on syntax, ordering, and semantic constraints, motivating generate–validate–repair designs. Prior empirical work varies by model set, task realism, and verifier integration, leaving unresolved how much marginal benefit verifiers provide in tightly controlled, preregistered paired tests. This study situates a preregistered paired test in that literature by measuring the guarded pipeline's marginal effect in a single‑model, emulation‑grounded regime.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and sampling. We preregistered CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 and froze sampling, analysis, timeouts, retry, and inclusion/exclusion rules prior to execution. Confirmatory sampling: N=200 multi‑device intents stratified into three topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. Model and generation. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json) and the preregistered execution used a single shared initial generation per intent (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; independent_condition_generation = false). The guarded pipeline allowed at most one verifier‑guided repair iteration per intent. Validator and pass rule. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) combines three ordered checks and assigns a binary verifier_pass when the post‑validation state passes all checks: (1) parsing/normalization—canonicalize generated commands and extract parsed command objects and counts; (2) task‑payload constraints—verify required‑sequence presence, preserved‑state constraints, and match against expected_final_state encoded in the task payload; (3) formal reachability/policy checks—run Batfish on the emulated topology and translate reachability/policy counterexamples into violation codes. The validator deterministically sets verifier_pass when validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the archived validator_trace for an episode (representative validator_trace files are in execution/scoring/ and execution/responses/). Execution environment and logging. Execution used containerized Mininet‑style emulation with FRRouting and VyOS images, Batfish as the verifier, and deterministic task generation. Timeouts, retries, missingness and multiplicity rules followed the preregistration. All raw model responses, validator traces, and run logs were archived (see execution/ and analysis/ paths in the artifact bundle). Statistical analysis and detectability note. The preregistered primary test is the exact two‑sided McNemar test on paired binary semantic‑error outcomes (alpha = 0.05) with the primary estimand the absolute paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline). A 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10000) was preregistered for the paired difference. Important detectability tradeoff: when the design uses a shared_initial_candidate for both conditions, baseline and guarded can be identical unless the guarded branch applies a repair; this controls generation variance but reduces sensitivity to marginal repair effects because the only way to create discordant pairs is for the guarded pipeline to change the shared candidate. We address the statistical consequences of this choice in Results and Statistical‑Interpretation.
sections.results: Execution accounting and basic outcomes. Execution completed per plan: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 baseline + 200 guarded), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0 (execution summary in execution/execution_manifest.json). The analysis artifacts record complete_pair_count = 200 and the paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The paired absolute success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) estimate = 0.00 with preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10000; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Repair attempts and shared_initial identity (artifact‑grounded facts). The preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced a single shared initial LLM candidate that was used for both baseline and guarded conditions. For all 200 confirmatory pairs the shared initial candidate was identical to both the baseline and guarded raw responses (shared_initial_candidate_sha256 == baseline_raw_response_sha256 == guarded_raw_response_sha256 for 200/200 pairs); representative per‑task files showing identical shared/baseline/guarded responses include execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt, and execution/responses/task-000001-guarded.txt (see execution/representative_tasks/ and execution/scoring/ entries). Because the shared initial candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator for every confirmatory episode (validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0), no verifier‑guided repair was ever applied in the confirmatory cohort (repair_applied == false in every archived validator_trace; repair attempts = 0/200). These counts are recorded across the execution and analysis artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json and analysis/condition_summary.csv). Statistical contingency and inference vacuity. The observed contingency (n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) makes the preregistered McNemar test uninformative for detecting marginal repair effects: with zero discordant pairs the McNemar statistic yields p = 1.0 but provides no signal about potential marginal improvements that would appear under different generation semantics or task/model regimes. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] because resampling identical paired outcomes reproduces zero differences. Representative difficulty diagnostics. Representative statistics from six archived exemplars included in the artifact bundle (execution/representative_tasks/) show changed_interface_count = {1,2,2,2,2,2} (mean = 1.83, median = 2); required_command_count = {4,2,6,4,3,6} (mean = 4.17, median = 4); dependency_rule_count commonly = 2; difficulty labels include medium/hard/very_hard. Contamination and exclusions. The preregistered contamination filters flagged zero exact‑hash duplicates and no high n‑gram overlap within the confirmatory N; no confirmatory episodes were excluded (analysis/contamination_summary.csv and execution/task_manifest.jsonl).
sections.discussion: Why the confirmatory test was uninformative. The preregistered shared_initial_generation design intentionally controlled for generation variance by using a single initial candidate per intent for both conditions. That design reduces variance due to model randomness but requires the guarded repair stage to modify that shared candidate to produce discordant pairs. In this run the shared candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator in every confirmatory episode; hence the guarded branch had no opportunity to apply repairs and the confirmatory test could not detect a marginal verifier benefit. McNemar and bootstrap inference are therefore vacuous under the observed contingency (n10 = n01 = 0): p = 1.0 and the bootstrap CI collapses to a point. Validator ↔ emulator correspondence and construct limits. Within the archived artifacts, validator_pass corresponded to deterministic validator checks (parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests) and emulation results: validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 aligned with emulation success for all confirmatory episodes. However, the validator and emulation used FRRouting/VyOS images and cannot capture all hardware timing/race quirks or vendor‑specific idiosyncrasies. Threats to validity and implications. Key limitations that constrain external generalization include single model family (gpt‑5‑mini only), limited vendor/device diversity (FRR/VyOS only), synthetic deterministic task generation, emulator fidelity limits, and the preregistered detectability tradeoff induced by shared_initial_generation. Operational implication: the absence of an observed marginal verifier benefit here should not be read as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary. Rather, it demonstrates that marginal repair utility depends on experimental factors (generation semantics, model diversity, adversarial task selection, emulator fidelity). Recommendations for future evaluations. To expose potential marginal verifier utility, future preregistered studies should consider: (a) independent per‑condition generation or multiple independent generations per intent to increase opportunities for repair to act, (b) multi‑model evaluations to capture model heterogeneity, (c) broader vendor image diversity or real‑device testbeds, (d) adversarial/noisy intent banks to surface failure modes, and (e) trace‑centered metrics (tool calls, counterexample provenance, rollback correctness) in addition to final binary pass/fail.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation comparing a bounded verifier‑in‑the‑loop generate–validate–repair pipeline to single‑pass LLM generation for NL→config translation in emulated multi‑device networks, both baseline and guarded conditions deterministically passed the preregistered validator for all confirmatory intents (n11 = 200; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The guarded repair stage was never invoked (repair attempts = 0/200) because the shared initial LLM candidate already satisfied validator checks for every confirmatory episode; therefore the preregistered primary paired test (McNemar) was uninformative for marginal repair detection (p = 1.0; paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). We provide artifact‑grounded counts and validator decision rules that substantiate this outcome (see execution/scoring/, execution/responses/, and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). To evaluate practical marginal utility of verifier‑guided repair in NetOps, future work must broaden model and device diversity, use independent per‑condition or multiple generations to increase detectability, include adversarial intents, and adopt trace‑centered evaluation metrics rather than relying solely on final pass/fail under a shared‑candidate design.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). The study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration manifest referenced in execution/execution_manifest.json; preregistration_sha256 = 163150627c4bd8d1e2520caeaa8ac0f4e0aa78876c16c3246e91596c632e49ec). Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish used as the formal verifier; deterministic task generator; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The validator assigns verifier_pass when the archived validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the validator_trace (this combines parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests as described in Methods and recorded in execution/scoring/*.json). The confirmatory run used a shared initial generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice that intentionally controls generation variance and produced the observed detectability tradeoff. All experiment orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts (refer to execution/ and analysis/ paths in the bundle) for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or families.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic deterministic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture full operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies, timing, or race conditions of production devices.

Design detectability tradeoff: shared_initial_generation (shared initial candidate for baseline and guarded) was chosen to control generation variance but reduces sensitivity to detect marginal repair benefits (a principal internal‑validity limitation).
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inference.

Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero matches in confirmatory N and n‑gram overlap detectors reported no high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
